headline: High Court refused MACC's bid to freeze RM548m linked to Na'imah in Singapore
context: On 22 May 2026, the KL High Court refused MACC's bid for a Section 53 order to freeze £21 million and US$99 million (about RM548m) held in Singapore and alleged to be linked to Na'imah Abdul Khalid, widow of the late Tun Daim Zainuddin, and eight others. MACC says it will appeal.

changes.summary: Correction: this card said a London court granted, then stayed, a £132m freeze; the KL High Court granted that freeze over London assets in June 2025 and stayed it three weeks later, and on 30 June 2026 ruled it had expired.
Correction: we now say two legal questions in the widow's asset-declaration case were referred to the Federal Court in March 2026, rather than that the case itself is before that court.

cards.big: MACC's hunt for assets linked to Daim Zainuddin's family looked sweeping: RM3 billion traced across 11 countries, Ilham Tower seized, accounts chased from London to Singapore.
cards.sub: Then on 22 May 2026 a judge refused to freeze about RM548m of it in Singapore, and spelled out where the case fell short.

cards.big: High Court judge Mohd Arief Emran Arifin dismissed the bid, ruling the prosecution had not met the threshold Section 53 of the anti-money-laundering act sets.
cards.sub: Section 53 lets a court bar dealing with assets held abroad while a case runs. The judge found the evidence for that bar too thin.

cards.big: Malaysia's drive to lock down the overseas money keeps meeting court limits: the KL High Court granted a £132m London freeze in June 2025, then stayed it.
cards.sub: On 30 June 2026 the same court ruled the London order had expired by operation of law. MACC said it would appeal the Singapore refusal.

cards.big: Announced scope is not proven guilt. Daim was discharged and acquitted after his death; the wider case remains unproven.
cards.sub: Na'imah contests a 2024 asset-declaration charge; two of its legal questions went to the Federal Court in March 2026. The ruling judged the freeze, not whether the money is clean.

cards.big: A seizure announced is not money recovered. Between the press conference and the recovered ringgit sits a proof threshold the state has yet to clear.
Think of it as tracing money you suspect is tainted, then being told you have not shown enough to stop the account holders touching it while the case runs.
Asset recovery turns on proving provenance to the law's threshold, not the size of the number announced. The appeal decides whether the money can be frozen, not who keeps it.
